title: Net overseas migration in 2022–23 was roughly double the average of the decade before the pandemic
oneLiner: The post-pandemic intake was far above any previous year.
body: The Bureau of Statistics recorded net overseas migration above 500,000 in 2022–23, against an average of a little over 200,000 a year across 2010 to 2019. It was the largest annual intake on record by a wide margin.
contextBackground: The number is the starting point of the current debate, and both sides use it. It is cited by supporters of a cap as evidence the system is out of control and by opponents as evidence of an obvious one-off.
contextDisagreement: The figure itself is not contested. Its meaning is: whether it describes a new normal or a rebound.

otherClaim.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year

claimItself.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the federal government should cap net arrivals below the levels of the past decade and well below the post-pandemic peak.
claimItself.body: Net overseas migration is arrivals minus departures of people who stay, or leave, for at least twelve months. It averaged just over 200,000 a year in the decade before the pandemic and exceeded 500,000 in 2022–23. The proposal is a cap of 200,000, which would require the government to manage the student, temporary-work and permanent programs together to hit it.

claimItself.title: New housing completions have not kept pace with population growth in Australia's largest cities over the past decade
claimItself.oneLiner: Dwellings built per new resident have fallen, and vacancy rates in Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and Perth sit near record lows.
claimItself.body: Completions peaked around 2017 and fell through the pandemic as costs rose and builders failed, while population growth resumed at pace. The national housing agency's projections show a cumulative shortfall against household formation through the second half of the decade.
